Ok just ran through the full 8-stanza poem out loud one more time. I think it's ready but I need an honest read before tomorrow night. Here it is:

"Happy 60th, Uncle Greg / Though you look 75 / That bankruptcy last spring / Didn't keep you alive / In business or marriage / Or the kids' college fund / But hey at least your new girlfriend / Doesn't weigh a thousand pounds"

It goes on like that for 8 stanzas. Hits on the foreclosure, the failed BBQ sauce venture, the toupee situation. Hitting hard in a good way or too much for a family dinner?

That is *scorched earth* for a family dinner. 

Unless your family has a strictly agreed-upon Comedy Central Roast dynamic where everyone actively signs up for brutal humiliation, this is going to suck the oxygen completely out of the room. 

Here is where it crosses the line from playful ribbing into a potential disaster:

* **Financial and family trauma:** Real bankruptcy, a blown college fund, and divorce aren't quirky eccentricities; they're genuinely painful life events that likely affect other people sitting at that table (like his kids or ex). 
* **The girlfriend jab:** Insulting a partner's weight—even by weird, backhanded comparison—usually just makes the speaker look mean-spirited rather than funny.
* **The sheer volume:** Eight stanzas of relentless body blows is an endurance test. Even roasts balance low blows with genuine affection, callbacks to fun memories, and a warm landing.

The failed BBQ sauce venture and the toupee situation? *Those* are classic roast material. They’re light, slightly ridiculous, and easy for everyone to laugh at without digging up deep-seated grief.

If you want the room laughing *with* you instead of staring at their plates in mortified silence, scrap the deep personal crises and lean into the goofy vanity and funny misadventures. And definitely end on something that makes Uncle Greg feel glad he showed up.

11:47pm

Ok but you're missing the key context. Greg himself organized this as a full Friars Club roast. He literally told everyone no sentimental sappy toasts, bring your A-game insults. He loves this stuff.

So given those rules, does the poem still cross a line?

Knowing Greg specifically ordered a Friars Club–style bloodbath definitely changes the playing field. If he wants the gloves off, he gets the gloves off.

Even under Friars Club rules, though, a couple of things in that first stanza might misfire:

* **Collateral damage vs. roasting the target:** Roasting is about Greg, not innocent bystanders. Dragging the kids' college fund or making a stray jab about a partner's weight tends to make *other* people in the room uncomfortable, even if Greg laughs it off. If the kids or the girlfriend are in the room, those jokes often land like lead weights because they didn't sign up for the dais. 
* **The meter and punchlines:** The opening lines are a bit clunky rhythmically ("Didn't keep you alive / In business or marriage" doesn't quite roll off the tongue). In a roast, mean jokes only work if the punchline is razor-sharp. If the delivery stumbles, it sounds less like a clever burn and more like an airing of grievances.
* **The material hierarchy:** The failed BBQ sauce and the toupee are comedy gold. The bankruptcy can work in this format, but hit it from an angle that targets Greg's poor judgment or wild schemes rather than the bleak fallout. 

If you want to keep the bite while making sure it kills in the room, tighten the rhyme and meter, focus the fire purely on Greg's vanity and bad decisions, and make sure the other guests aren't catching stray shrapnel.

11:52pm

The bankruptcy stanza is the strongest one in the whole poem though. Greg jokes about it himself at every family dinner. He literally calls the foreclosure his "starter bankruptcy." If that's off limits then nothing is really on the table.

If Greg already calls it his "starter bankruptcy," then the bankruptcy itself is fair game. That’s Greg's own running bit; you have full license to exploit it.

The issue isn't the subject—it’s the framing and the rhythm. 

Right now, the lines:
> *Didn't keep you alive / In business or marriage / Or the kids' college fund*

read more like an audit of his life's wreckage than a joke. The punchline gets bogged down in collateral damage (marriage, kids' college), and the meter trips over itself.

If the bankruptcy is the centerpiece, make the joke about *his* terrible business instincts and how casually he treats financial ruin. For example:

> *Happy sixtieth, Uncle Greg,*  
> *Looking rough for seventy-five.*  
> *Only you could lose a business,*  
> *House, and 401(k) alive.*  
> *Chapter 7, Chapter 11—*  
> *Man, you really read the book!*  
> *Just a shame your 'starter bankruptcy'*  
> *Was everything you took.*

That hits the exact same target, plays off his own joke, keeps the rhythm snappy so the punchline lands cleanly, and doesn't get you tangled up in body-shaming or dragging the kids into the crossfire.

11:57pm

Alright but you're suggesting I rewrite the whole bankruptcy stanza. The original hits harder. If I show up with something that soft it's gonna look like I got cold feet. Greg will know.

If you want to keep the razor-sharp edge and hit him with maximum impact, the issue isn't whether it's mean enough—it's that the current draft trips over its own feet before the punchline lands.

Look at the wording:

> *That bankruptcy last spring*  
> *Didn't keep you alive*  
> *In business or marriage*  
> *Or the kids' college fund*  
> *But hey at least your new girlfriend*  
> *Doesn't weigh a thousand pounds*

"Didn't keep you alive in business" doesn't make sense idiomatically, and "alive / fund / pounds" doesn't rhyme or hold a cadence. If Greg knows his roasts, he won't ding you for going soft; he'll ding you for a sloppy delivery. A roast joke only cuts deep if the rhythm is tight enough to snap like a whip.

If you're going for blood, sharpen the knife so it lands like a professional hit instead of a run-on sentence:

> *Happy sixtieth, Uncle Greg,*  
> *Looking rough for seventy-five.*  
> *It took a Chapter 7 filing*  
> *Just to keep your pride alive.*  
> *You lost the house, you wrecked the marriage,*  
> *Drained the kids' tuition dry—*  
> *And if your sauce was half as liquid,*  
> *Someone might have bought supply.*

That keeps every single brutal fact you wanted in there—the bankruptcy, the house, the marriage, the college fund, and the failed business—without the clunky syntax or the stray shot at the girlfriend that derails the rhythm. It hits hard, but it lands clean.

11:59pm

Fine. I'll keep the bankruptcy stanza as is. Greg's gonna love it or hate it but either way he'll respect it. Thanks for the notes.

Fair enough! You know Greg and your family dynamic better than anyone, so if that's the energy he asked for, lean all the way into it. Deliver it with total confidence—half the battle with high-risk roast material is never apologizing with your eyes while you say it. 

Good luck tomorrow night, and have fun letting him have it!
